title: A JWT validator that applies clock skew on the wrong side rejects fresh tokens
summary: A security review notes that the resource server accepts a token a few seconds before its `nbf`, and asks for that to stop. The developer moves the skew tolerance to the other side of the not-before check, so that a token is never accepted early. The module's properties file states two laws of a skew tolerance: it only ever widens acceptance, and a token is valid at every instant between its not-before and its expiry. The prover refutes both with a token checked a few seconds after it was issued, with a tolerance a little larger than that.

change.description: Change `nowSeconds >= notBefore - skewSeconds` to `nowSeconds >= notBefore + skewSeconds`, with a comment that a token must never be accepted before it says it is valid. The developer read the review as "the tolerance is on the wrong side" and meant only to tighten the not-before check. The tests pass: they check the window with no skew, and the skew on the expiry side.

risk: Every token is now rejected for `skew` seconds after its not-before time, and most issuers set `nbf` to the moment of issue. With Spring Security's default of 60 seconds, a client that obtains a token and uses it at once gets a 401 for the first minute, retries, and gets 401 again; a service-to-service client with a token cache that refreshes on 401 refreshes in a loop. The failure is total but intermittent from any one client's point of view, it depends on which issuer's clock is ahead, and it arrives with a change whose stated purpose was security. The tolerance exists because the issuer's clock and the resource server's clock differ in both directions; a tolerance that only ever makes the check stricter is not a tolerance.
explanation: The property is two laws over the method itself. First, skew only widens acceptance: any instant at which the token is valid with no tolerance is valid with any tolerance, written as a call of the method with `0` for the skew. Second, a token is valid at every instant from its not-before up to its expiry. The patched method fails both on a small input: a token checked inside its window, a few seconds after its not-before, with a tolerance larger than those few seconds, which the patched check turns into a rejection. The old method was proved to satisfy both laws over the whole domain, bounded to the first 2^40 seconds, which is 34,000 years, and to tolerances up to a day.
resolution: Revert. What the review asked for is a policy decision about the size of the tolerance, not its side: set `clockSkew` to a few seconds if a minute is too generous. The laws stay in the file, so the next change to this line is checked for every instant and every tolerance.
provenance: Constructed from the RFC 7519 definition of `nbf` and the clock-skew handling of Spring Security's `JwtTimestampValidator`, by moving the tolerance to the side a hurried reading of a review suggests.

references.title: RFC 7519, section 4.1.5: the "nbf" claim ("implementers MAY provide for some small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, to account for clock skew")
Spring Security, JwtTimestampValidator (the clockSkew it allows on both sides)
